---
title: Configuration
---

pycmdcheck reads its settings from the `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the
`pyproject.toml` in the directory it checks.

One kind of run does not. A run that is given a settings file with `--config`
takes everything from that file and does not read the table.
[A Settings File Outside the Project](#config-file) at the end of this page
describes the file.

## Basic Configuration

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck]
# Exit with code 1 on warnings as well as on errors
fail_on = ["warning"]

[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]
# Every check is enabled by default. List only the ones you want to
# turn off or configure.
urls = false
tests = { runner = "pytest", args = ["-x"] }
```

A [profile](cli.qmd#profiles) replaces the enable flags with its own check
set, and its options win over the same options here.
[Precedence](cli.qmd#precedence) in the command-line reference gives the full
order.

A mistake in this table does not stop the run. pycmdcheck prints a warning on
standard error in each of these cases.

- `pyproject.toml` cannot be read. The defaults are used.
- `fail_on` is not a list, or one of its entries is not a valid status. That
  value is ignored.
- A check is set to something other than `true`, `false` or a table. The check
  stays enabled.
- A name under `[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]` matches no check. The name is
  ignored.

The table has two keys, `fail_on` and `checks`. Any other key is ignored
without a warning. A profile, for one, is chosen with `--profile` and cannot
be set here.

There is one warning line for each kind of mistake, and the line names the
values or entries that have it. This table has three kinds.

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck]
fail_on = ["warnings"]

[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]
linting = "ruff"
typing = "mypy"
licence = false
```

A run prints these three lines on standard error.

```
Config: Invalid fail_on value "warnings". Valid values: error, note, warning
Config: Each entry in 'checks' should be true, false, or a table. Ignoring the value of: linting (str), typing (str)
Ignoring unknown check name(s) in [tool.pycmdcheck.checks]: licence
```

A line that starts with `Config:` names at most 25 values or entries and then
says how many are left, as in `and 3 more`. The line about `checks` names the
built-in checks first, so a long list of other names cannot hide one.

The options inside a check's table get no such warning, because each check
reads its own options when it runs. When one of the six
[tool checks](#options-shared-by-the-tool-checks) cannot use its `args`,
`timeout`, `tool` or `runner` value, it says so in its own result.
For every other option, a value of the wrong type passes without a message.
Where a number is expected, any other value is ignored and the default is
used. Where `true` or `false` is expected, any non-empty string counts as
`true`, so `check_docstrings = "no"` turns the docstring scan on.

A [settings file](#config-file) given with `--config` is read strictly.
There a mistake of any of these kinds is a usage error, and no check runs.

## Global Options

### `fail_on` {#fail_on}

A list that names the status from which the run exits with code 1. The valid
values are `"error"`, `"warning"` and `"note"`. The default is `["error"]`.

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck]
fail_on = ["warning"]
```

The value is a threshold, as it is for [`--fail-on`](cli.qmd#fail-on). A
status brings every more severe status with it.

| Setting | Statuses that fail the run |
|---------|----------------------------|
| `fail_on = ["error"]` | error |
| `fail_on = ["warning"]` | warning and error |
| `fail_on = ["note"]` | note, warning and error |

When the list names several statuses, the least severe one counts, so
`["error", "warning"]` means the same as `["warning"]`. The list takes effect
when `--fail-on` is not given on the command line. A `--fail-on` option
replaces the list. `--exit-zero` keeps the exit code at 0 whatever either
says. The closing line of the report still follows the threshold, and so
does the `failed` key of the report that `--json` prints. An invalid entry
is ignored with a warning. A run with `--config` does not read the list. It
uses the `fail_on` of the [settings file](#config-file).

## Check Configuration

A check takes either a boolean or a table.

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]
linting = false                              # turn a check off
typing = { tool = "mypy", strict = true }    # configure a check
docs = { enabled = false }                   # the table form of "off"
```

`enabled` defaults to `true` in the table form. A check named with `--check`,
or `-c` for short, runs whatever `enabled` says, and so does a check that a
profile selects.

### Options Shared by the Tool Checks

The `build`, `doctests`, `formatting`, `linting`, `tests` and `typing` checks
each start an external tool. They share two options.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments, added at the end of the tool's command line |
| `timeout` | positive number | see each check | Seconds the tool may run before it is stopped |

`args` must be a list with one string for each argument. Any other value, a
single string included, gives an error result with the message
`Invalid args option`. A `timeout` that is not a positive number is ignored
and the default is used, with a detail line that says so. A value above 86400
seconds, which is 24 hours, is lowered to that.

### Choosing the Tool {#tool-auto}

The `formatting`, `linting` and `typing` checks also have a `tool` option. Its
default is `"auto"`, which runs the tool the project itself has configured.
Each check finds that out from the project's files, and its section below
lists the files and tables it looks for. A project that has configured no
tool for a check is skipped, with a message such as `No linter configured`
and the [skip reason](rules.qmd#skip-reasons) `not-configured`. pycmdcheck
does not hold a project to a linter, a type checker or a formatter that the
project never chose.

That reason means the configuration was read and names no tool. When
`pyproject.toml` cannot be read, and no other file such as `ruff.toml` or
`mypy.ini` selects a tool, the check cannot tell. It is then skipped with the
message `pyproject.toml could not be read` and the reason
`prerequisite-failed`, and the `metadata` check reports the broken file.

A tool that you name always runs, whatever the project has configured.

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]
linting = { tool = "ruff" }
typing = { tool = "mypy" }
formatting = { tool = "ruff" }
```

A `tool` value the check does not know is an error. The result carries a
[hint](rules.qmd#findings) that lists the values, and `--verbose`, or `-v`
for short, prints it as a suggestion. This is
`pycmdcheck --check typing --verbose` on a project that sets
`typing = { tool = "pyre" }`.

```
│  ✗  │ typing │ Unsupported type checker: pyre │ 0.00s │
└─────┴────────┴────────────────────────────────┴───────┘

typing details:
  Suggestion: Set tool in [tool.pycmdcheck.checks.typing] to "auto", "mypy" or "pyright".
```

A run with `--config` does not read this table. There the tool is named in
the [settings file](#config-file), in the same form under `[checks]`.

The [`strict` profile](cli.qmd#profiles) names ruff for `linting` and mypy for
`typing`. A profile's options win over `pyproject.toml`, so under
`--profile strict` those two tools run on every project, also on one whose
`pyproject.toml` cannot be read, and a `tool` option set here for either
check is replaced. The `pyopensci` and `core` profiles set no tool, so
detection applies under them.

### A Tool That Is Missing or Cannot Run {#tool-could-not-run}

The six checks treat a tool that did not do its job in the same way.

| Situation | Status | Message | Skip reason or code |
|-----------|--------|---------|---------------------|
| The tool is not installed | skipped | `ruff not installed`, with a detail line that says how to install it | `tool-missing` |
| The tool is installed and could not run | warning | `ruff could not run` | `linting.could-not-run` |
| The tool ran longer than `timeout` | error | `Linting timed out` | `linting.timed-out` |

The messages name the tool or the check, so `ruff` and `Linting` stand for
whichever applies, and each code starts with the name of the check.

For ruff and for the `build` module, the detail line names the pycmdcheck
extra that installs the tool, as in `pip install "pycmdcheck[linting]"`.
pycmdcheck has five extras, which are `linting`, `typing-mypy`,
`typing-pyright`, `build` and `all`.
[Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#optional-dependencies) says what each
one installs and why pytest has none.

A tool could not run when it cannot be started, when it crashes, or when it
rejects its arguments or its configuration. That says nothing about the
project's code, which is why it is a warning and not an error. With the
default `fail_on` it does not make pycmdcheck exit with code 1. The detail
lines give the exit code, as in `mypy exited with code 2`, and the end of
what the tool printed, at most 10 lines. When the tool could not be started
they give the reason.

The `tests` check has one case of its own. A test suite that pytest cannot
collect is an error, as its [section](#tests) explains.

[Getting Started](getting-started.qmd#tools-the-checks-need) says which tool
each check needs and where pycmdcheck looks for it.

Some of the tools write into the project. pytest leaves a `.pytest_cache`
directory and mypy leaves `.mypy_cache`. The build check sends the built files
to a temporary directory, but a build backend may still write into the source
tree, as setuptools does with its `*.egg-info` directory. ruff is run without
its cache.

The linting check does not let ruff apply fixes. It passes `--no-fix` and
`--no-fix-only` to ruff after every other argument, and ruff follows the last
one it is given. Neither `fix = true` or `fix-only = true` in the project's
ruff configuration, nor `--fix` in `args`, changes that.

ruff arguments that write a file or never finish are refused. With
`--add-noqa`, `--output-file` or `--watch` in `args`, or their short forms
`-o` and `-w`, the check returns ERROR "Invalid args option" and ruff is not
started.

The `args` of all six checks are read from the `pyproject.toml` of the
project being checked. Look at them before you run these checks on a
repository you did not write. A run with `--config` takes them from the
[settings file](#config-file) and not from the project.

## Per-Check Options

The sections are in the order `pycmdcheck --list` uses. A check with no
options still accepts `true`, `false` and `enabled`.

### build

Builds the package with `python -m build` and looks for a wheel or a source
distribution in the output. The `build` module must be installed in the
environment that runs pycmdcheck.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for `python -m build` |
| `timeout` | positive number | `120` | Seconds the build may take |

```toml
build = { args = ["--wheel"], timeout = 300 }
```

A build that fails is an error. A build that
[could not run](#tool-could-not-run), for example because `args` holds an
argument that `python -m build` does not know, is a warning with the message
`build could not run`.

The check is skipped in three cases and starts no build in any of them.

| Situation | Message | Skip reason |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| The `build` module is not installed | `'build' module not installed` | `tool-missing` |
| `pyproject.toml` cannot be read, also when a `setup.py` sits beside it | `pyproject.toml could not be read` | `prerequisite-failed` |
| The project has none of `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py` and `setup.cfg` | `No pyproject.toml found` | `prerequisite-failed` |

In the last two cases the `metadata` check reports the cause. The module is
looked for first, so a project with a broken `pyproject.toml` is skipped as
`tool-missing` where the module is not installed.

### changelog

Looks for a changelog. No options.

It accepts a file named `CHANGELOG`, `CHANGES`, `NEWS`, `HISTORY`, `RELEASES`,
`RELEASE_NOTES` or `WHATSNEW`, in any letter case, with a `.md`, `.rst` or
`.txt` extension or none, in the project root, `docs/` or `doc/`. It also
accepts a directory of release notes named `changes/`, `newsfragments/` or
`changelog.d/`, and a changelog link in `[project.urls]`. When the only file
found is in the root and has fewer than 50 characters, the result is a note
that the changelog is too short. A file in the root that cannot be read is a
warning with the code `changelog.unreadable` when nothing else counts as a
changelog. That holds with a short file beside it, and a detail line then
names the short file.

### ci

Looks for the configuration file of a continuous integration (CI) service. No
options.

It knows GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Travis CI, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure
Pipelines, Buildkite, AppVeyor, Cirrus CI, Woodpecker CI, Forgejo Actions,
Gitea Actions, Bitbucket Pipelines, Drone and sourcehut. It reports that a
file is present and does not read what the configuration runs.

### citation

Looks for a citation file, or for other metadata that says how to cite the
project. No options.

The check first looks in the project root for a file named `CITATION`, in any
letter case, with a `.cff`, `.bib`, `.md`, `.txt` or `.rst` extension or none.
For a `CITATION.cff` it also reports which of the four keys the Citation File
Format requires (`cff-version`, `message`, `title`, `authors`) it found.

Without such a file, any one of these also passes, with the message
`Citation metadata found`.

- A `.zenodo.json` file in the project root.
- A `codemeta.json` file in the project root.
- A paper for the Journal of Open Source Software, which is a `paper.md` with
  a `paper.bib` in the same directory. The directory may be the project root,
  `paper/` or `joss/`.
- A README in the project root that links a Digital Object Identifier (DOI).
  A link to `doi.org/10.` counts, and so does a Zenodo badge link.

The names are matched in any letter case. The detail lines say what was
found, for example
`Found: paper/paper.md with paper/paper.bib (a Journal of Open Source Software paper)`.
A project with none of these gets a note.

### community

Looks for a contributing guide and a code of conduct. No options.

The names are `CONTRIBUTING`, and `CODE_OF_CONDUCT`, `CODE-OF-CONDUCT` or
`CONDUCT`, in any letter case, with a `.md`, `.rst` or `.txt` extension or
none. They may be in the project root, `.github/`, `docs/` or `doc/`. Default
files that an organization keeps in its own `.github` repository are not part
of a clone, so this check cannot see them.

### dependencies

Compares the third-party modules the package imports with the dependencies
declared in `pyproject.toml`. No options.

An import at module level that no dependency accounts for is a warning, and a
detail line names the first file that imports each such module. A declared
dependency that is never imported is a note. Imports that are guarded, for
example inside `try`/`except ImportError`, inside a function, or under
`if TYPE_CHECKING`, are listed and not flagged. Extras and development
dependencies count as declared.

The check imports and executes nothing. To learn which modules a dependency
provides, it reads the metadata of the packages installed next to pycmdcheck
and otherwise goes by the dependency's name. Run it from the project's
environment for the most exact answer.

The check is skipped when it has nothing to compare.

| Situation | Skip reason |
|-----------|-------------|
| `pyproject.toml` is missing, cannot be read, or has neither a `[project]` nor a `[tool.poetry]` table | `prerequisite-failed` |
| `dependencies` or `optional-dependencies` is listed in `dynamic` | `not-applicable` |
| No source file of the package was found | `not-applicable` |

Source files that were found and could not be parsed are a different matter,
because the author can fix them. When none of them can be parsed the result
is a note.

### docs

Looks for a README. When asked, it also looks for documentation beyond the
README and measures docstring coverage.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `require_readme` | boolean | `true` | Report a missing README as a warning |
| `check_readme_sections` | boolean | `false` | Report a README that does not appear to mention installation or usage |
| `check_docs_site` | boolean | `false` | Report a project that has no documentation beyond its README |
| `check_docstrings` | boolean | `false` | Report public modules, classes and functions that have no docstring |
| `min_docstring_coverage` | number from 0 to 100 | `0` | Share of public items, in percent, that must have a docstring |

```toml
docs = { check_readme_sections = true, min_docstring_coverage = 80 }
```

A `min_docstring_coverage` above 0 turns the docstring scan on, whether or not
`check_docstrings` is set, and becomes the pass mark. Coverage at or above it
passes, and coverage below it is a note. When a file of the sample could not
be parsed and no public item was counted, there is no coverage to compare,
and the result is a note with the code `docs.docstrings-not-counted`. With
`check_docstrings = true` and no minimum, any public item without a docstring
is a note. The scan reads at most 20 files, spread evenly across the package,
and says so when it left files out. Names that start with an underscore are
not counted.

The README may be in the project root, `.github/` or `docs/`, in any letter
case, or be declared with `readme` in `pyproject.toml`. A README that is found
and cannot be read is a warning with the code `docs.unreadable-readme`, also
with `require_readme = false`. Its length and its installation and usage text
are then not checked.

With `check_docs_site = true` the check looks for documentation beyond the
README. Any one of these is enough.

1. The setup of a site builder. In the project root that is a Read the Docs
   file (`.readthedocs.yml` or `readthedocs.yml`), `mkdocs.yml`,
   `zensical.toml`, `_quarto.yml`, `myst.yml` or `_toc.yml`. In `docs/`,
   `doc/` or `documentation/` it is a Sphinx `conf.py`, also in a `source/`
   directory there, or one of `mkdocs.yml`, `_quarto.yml`, `myst.yml` and
   `_toc.yml`. A name that ends in `.yml` may end in `.yaml` as well.
2. A page in `docs/`, `doc/` or `documentation/`, at any depth. A page is a
   file that ends in `.md`, `.rst`, `.qmd`, `.ipynb` or `.adoc`. A file or a
   directory named `README`, `CONTRIBUTING`, `CODE_OF_CONDUCT`, `SECURITY`,
   `SUPPORT`, `CHANGELOG`, `GOVERNANCE`, `ISSUE_TEMPLATE` or
   `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE` does not count, since a project can keep those in
   `docs/` and have no other documentation. The file that `readme` in
   `pyproject.toml` names does not count either. A symbolic link to a
   directory is not followed.
3. A documentation link in the project metadata. A link counts when a word of
   its label ends in `doc`, `docs` or `documentation`, as in `Documentation`
   and `API docs`. Such a link does not count when it leads only to the front
   page or the README of a repository on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or
   Codeberg, because that page shows the README again. A link with any label
   counts when its address is on Read the Docs, GitHub Pages or GitLab Pages.
   The links are read from `[project.urls]` or the legacy Poetry keys, and
   from the `project_urls` and `url` of `setup.py` and `setup.cfg`.

Names are matched in any letter case. A project with none of the three gets a
note with the code `docs.missing-site` and the message
`No documentation beyond the README found`. When one is found, a detail line
names it, for example `Found documentation: docs/conf.py`.

The check cannot always read every link. A link may be set when the package
is built, which happens when `urls` is listed in `dynamic` and when
`setup.py` computes its `project_urls` or its `url`. A `pyproject.toml` or a
`setup.py` may also fail to parse. When one of these is the case and nothing
else was found, the project gets no note, and a detail line says that a
documentation link could not be looked for.

With `require_readme = false`, a project with no README has nothing for the
check to look at when the docstring scan counted nothing and
`check_docs_site` is off. The check is then skipped with the message
`No documentation to check` and the skip reason `not-applicable`. When the
scan counted nothing and a file of its sample could not be parsed, the
message is `Could not parse the package source` and the skip reason is
`parse-failed`, with or without a minimum.

The `triage`, `pyopensci` and `strict` [profiles](cli.qmd#profiles) each set
all five of these options, and their values then replace the ones given
here. All three turn `check_docs_site` on. `triage` turns the docstring scan
off with `check_docstrings = false` and `min_docstring_coverage = 0`, so a
project cannot switch it on for a triage run. `pyopensci` and `strict` turn
it on, with a minimum of 50 and of 80.

### doctests

Runs `pytest --doctest-modules` on the project's own packages and modules.
Needs pytest.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for pytest |
| `timeout` | positive number | `120` | Seconds the run may take |

A doctest is an example in a docstring. It is a line that starts with `>>>`,
with the result it should give on the lines below. The check returns one of
these results.

| What happened | Status | Message |
|---------------|--------|---------|
| Every example passed | ok | `All doctests passed` |
| An example failed | error | `2 doctest(s) failed` |
| The package has no doctests, or the project has no package or module to collect them from | skipped | `No doctests found` |
| No example ran, and pytest could not import some files | skipped | `No doctests ran, 2 files not imported` |
| pytest ended with exit code 2, 3 or 4, which mean a collection error, an internal error and a usage error | warning | `pytest could not run` |

A failed example is an error, so with the default `fail_on` the run exits
with code 1. Version 0.1.1 gave a warning. The last row is the shared rule
for a tool that [could not run](#tool-could-not-run). Unlike the `tests`
check, this check does not turn a collection error into an error.

The two skipped results of the table have different
[skip reasons](rules.qmd#skip-reasons). `No doctests found` has the reason
`not-applicable`, because the project gave the check nothing to look at.
`No doctests ran` has the reason `import-failed`. The files that were left
out may hold examples, and none of them ran. A run that does not fail then
ends with a [closing line](cli.qmd#text-output) such as
`No errors (1 skipped).` and not with `All checks passed!`.

The table leaves out the other results that all the
[tool checks](#options-shared-by-the-tool-checks) share. A missing pytest
gives a skipped result with the message `pytest not installed` and the reason
`tool-missing`. An `args` value that is not a list of strings and a run that
takes longer than `timeout` each give an error.

The first two messages also give the number of files that pytest could not
import, as in `All doctests passed, 1 file not imported`.

This is `pycmdcheck --check doctests --verbose` on a package with two wrong
examples. One of its modules, `maps.py`, imports a package that is not
installed.

```
│  ✗  │ doctests │ 2 doctest(s) failed, 1 file not imported │ 0.39s │
└─────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┴───────┘

doctests details:
  Running: pytest --doctest-modules
  Using pytest 9.0.2
  FAILED src/riverplot/__init__.py::riverplot.length - line 9: expected 3, got 2
  FAILED src/riverplot/__init__.py::riverplot.source - line 20: KeyError('Elbe')
  1 file could not be imported, so its examples did not run: src/riverplot/maps.py
  Suggestion: Correct each failed example or the code it calls, or mark an example that cannot run
    here with # doctest: +SKIP.
```

A docstring with a failed example gets a detail line of the form
`FAILED path::name - line N: reason`. The report shows at most 10 of these
lines and then says how many more there are. The path is the file. The name is the
function, class or module that the docstring belongs to, and N is the line of
the failed example in the file. pytest does not know that line for every
docstring. A function under `@functools.cache` is one such case, and the
reason then follows the name with no `line N:` before it. For a wrong result
the reason gives what the docstring expected and what the code gave. When the
result has several lines, it gives the first line that differs. Three dots
after what was expected or after what the code gave, as in
`expected left ..., got right ...`, mean that it has more lines than the one
shown. For an example that raised an error, the reason is the error, as in
`KeyError('Elbe')`. The reason is read from what pytest prints. When the
project changes that, for example with `--tb=no` in `args`, the line ends
after the name.

pytest counts a docstring as one test. A docstring gets one line however many
of its examples are wrong, with the line number and the reason of the first
one, and the number in the message counts docstrings. The details show the
first 10 of these lines. A line such as `... and 2 more` then says how many
were left out, and the message still counts them all. Unit tests that live
inside the package, in a file such as `src/riverplot/tests/test_core.py`, are
run by this check too, and a failed one is counted as a failed doctest.

The check passes `--doctest-ignore-import-errors` to pytest, so a file that
pytest cannot import is left out and its examples do not run. A common cause
is a module that imports an optional dependency which is not installed where
pycmdcheck runs. A file with a syntax error is left out in the same way. The
last detail line names such files. They add no finding and never give a
warning or an error, because the fault may be in the environment of the check
and not in the package. When no example ran at all, the result is skipped
with the reason `import-failed`. That is also the result when every example
of the other files is marked `# doctest: +SKIP`, although such a package
passes when no file is left out. The check reads this from the line where
pytest counts what passed, so the result is ok when the project turns that
line off, for example with `-q` in `args`.

pytest leaves a file out when the import fails with an `ImportError` or a
syntax error. A module that raises any other error when it is imported, such
as a `ValueError`, is not left out. pytest then stops with exit code 2, and
the result is the warning `pytest could not run` from the last row of the
table. Its details hold no `FAILED` line, so wrong examples in the other
files are not reported. A warning does not fail the run with the default
`fail_on`, so the exit code stays 0 when no other check gives an error.

#### Keeping an Example from Running

Some examples cannot run where the check runs, because they need the network,
a password or a large file. Put `# doctest: +SKIP` at the end of the example
line. The example stays in the docstring and is not run. The other examples
of the same docstring still run.

```python
def length(points):
    """Return how many points a river has.

    >>> length([(0, 0), (1, 2)])
    2
    >>> length(download("Rhine"))  # doctest: +SKIP
    1320
    """
    return len(points)
```

The module has no `download` function, so the second example would fail if
it ran. `pycmdcheck --check doctests` on this package passes.

```
│  ✓  │ doctests │ All doctests passed │
```

`# doctest: +SKIP` is the standard marker of Python's `doctest` module and
the counterpart of `\dontrun{}` in R. There is no counterpart of R's
`\donttest{}`, which marks an example that runs when a reader calls
`example()` and that `R CMD check` leaves out by default.

To leave a whole file out, pass pytest's `--ignore` option in `args`, with a
path relative to the project directory.

```toml
doctests = { args = ["--ignore=src/riverplot/maps.py"] }
```

With this line, the run further up no longer counts `maps.py`, and its
message is `2 doctest(s) failed`.

#### Running the Examples of a README

The check gives pytest only the project's packages and modules, so the
examples in a README do not run. Two arguments in `args` add them.

```toml
doctests = { args = ["--doctest-glob=*.md", "README.md"] }
```

`--doctest-glob=*.md` lets pytest read examples from a Markdown file, and
`README.md` names the file, with a path relative to the project directory.
A Markdown file inside the package is then read as well.

The examples of a README start with no names defined, so the README has to
import the package itself, as in `>>> from riverplot import length`. An
import that fails there is a failed example and so an error. It is not left
out as a module is. In a code block between two lines of backticks, leave an
empty line between the last example and the closing backticks. Without it,
pytest reads the backticks as part of the expected result.

pytest counts the whole README as one test. A wrong example gives one
`FAILED` line, which names the file twice and gives the line of the first
wrong example. This is `pycmdcheck --check doctests --verbose` on a package
with this setting whose README has a wrong example on line 7.

```
│  ✗  │ doctests │ 1 doctest(s) failed │ 1.57s │
└─────┴──────────┴─────────────────────┴───────┘

doctests details:
  Running: pytest --doctest-modules
  Using pytest 9.0.2
  FAILED README.md::README.md - line 7: expected 2, got 3
  Suggestion: Correct each failed example or the code it calls, or mark an example that cannot run
    here with # doctest: +SKIP.
```

### formatting

Runs a formatter in its checking mode, which changes no file. That is
`ruff format --check` or `black --check`.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `tool` | `"auto"`, `"ruff"`, `"black"` | `"auto"` | Formatter to check against |
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for the formatter |
| `timeout` | positive number | `120` | Seconds the formatter may run |

With `tool = "auto"` the check looks for a formatter the project has
configured, in this order.

1. ruff, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.ruff.format]` table, or when
   `ruff.toml` or `.ruff.toml` has a `[format]` section, a key that starts
   with `format.`, or the table on one line, as in
   `format = { quote-style = "single" }`.
2. black, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.black]` table.

A project with neither is skipped with the message `No formatter configured`
and the skip reason `not-configured`. Other ruff configuration does not
count, because a project can lint with ruff and not format with it. This is
`pycmdcheck --check linting,formatting` on a package whose only ruff
configuration is a `[tool.ruff.lint]` table. The two check names are
separated by a comma with no space after it, and the option can also be
[repeated](cli.qmd#selecting-checks).

```
│  ✓  │ linting    │ No linting issues found │
│  ○  │ formatting │ No formatter configured │
```

A project that formats with ruff at its default settings has no format table
either. To have it checked, add a `[tool.ruff.format]` table, which may be
empty, or name the tool.

```toml
formatting = { tool = "ruff" }
```

Files that would be reformatted are a warning. A formatter that
[could not run](#tool-could-not-run) is a warning as well.

### imports

Deprecated. Version 0.2.0 merged this check into
[`dependencies`](#dependencies), which reports undeclared imports from the
same scan. No options.

The name still works for one release. A run leaves the check out unless
`--check` or `checks=` names it, and it is then skipped with the message
`Merged into the dependencies check` and the skip reason `deprecated`. Remove
an `imports` entry from `[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]`, and run `dependencies`
where you ran `imports`. The
[command-line reference](cli.qmd#imports-check) shows the warning that such
an entry gives.

One answer changed with the merge. `imports` passed an undeclared module that
happened to be installed where pycmdcheck ran. `dependencies` reports every
undeclared module, installed or not.

### license

Looks for a license file and reports the license type. No options.

It accepts a file named `LICENSE`, `LICENCE`, `COPYING` or `UNLICENSE` in the
project root, in any letter case and with or without a suffix such as `.txt`
or `-MIT`. It also accepts files in a `LICENSE/` or `LICENSES/` directory, and
files named by `license-files` or `license.file` in `pyproject.toml`. A
project with no license file, or with one shorter than 50 characters, gets a
warning.

The type shown is the license declared in `pyproject.toml`, as a license
expression such as `MIT OR Apache-2.0` or else as a license classifier. With
neither, the check guesses from the text and says that it guessed.

The check also says whether the license is approved by the Open Source
Initiative (OSI). It takes the answer from a list that ships with pycmdcheck,
so it needs no network. The list is generated from the license list of the
System Package Data Exchange (SPDX), which marks each license identifier
that the OSI has approved. The script `tools/gen_osi_licenses.py` in the
pycmdcheck repository writes it to `src/pycmdcheck/_osi_licenses.py`.
`PSF-2.0` is added by hand, because the Python package index has an
OSI-approved classifier for it.

One case changes the status. When the declared license is an SPDX expression
and none of the licenses in it is on the list, the result is a note with the
code `license.not-osi-approved` and the message
`Declared license is not OSI-approved`. `CC-BY-NC-4.0` is such an expression.
One approved license is enough to pass, so `MIT OR CC-BY-NC-4.0` gets no
note.

Nothing else is graded. A declared word that is not an SPDX identifier, such
as `BSD`, a license classifier, and a type guessed from the license text each
get a detail line and leave the status alone. So does a declared value that
is not an expression, such as `MIT/Apache-2.0` or a sentence. Its line stands
above the type and reads
`Declared license: MIT/Apache-2.0 (not an SPDX expression)`. The same line
is shown when no license file is found or the file cannot be read. Beside a
file that cannot be read, a declared expression is shown as the type too. A
value longer than 200 characters or of more than one line, such as a license
text pasted under `license.text`, gets no line.

### linting

Runs a linter over the project.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `tool` | `"auto"`, `"ruff"`, `"flake8"`, `"pylint"` | `"auto"` | Linter to run |
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for the linter |
| `timeout` | positive number | `120`, or `300` for pylint | Seconds the linter may run |

```toml
linting = { tool = "ruff", args = ["--select", "E,F,W"] }
```

With `tool = "auto"` the check looks for a linter the project has configured,
in this order.

1. ruff, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.ruff]` table, or when the project
   has a `ruff.toml` or `.ruff.toml` file. A `[tool.ruff.lint]` table on its
   own counts, because it sits inside `[tool.ruff]`.
2. flake8, when the project has a `.flake8` file, or a `[flake8]` section in
   `setup.cfg` or `tox.ini`.
3. pylint, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.pylint]` table, or when the
   project has a `.pylintrc` or `pylintrc` file.

A project with none of these is skipped with the message
`No linter configured` and the skip reason `not-configured`. Under
`--profile strict` the tool is ruff, whatever the project has configured and
whatever `tool` says here.

Findings are a warning. A linter that [could not run](#tool-could-not-run),
for example because of an error in its configuration, is a warning as well,
with a message such as `ruff could not run`.

### metadata

Checks the project metadata in `pyproject.toml`. No options.

`name` and `version` are required, and a project without them is an error. So
is a `pyproject.toml` that cannot be parsed. `description`, `readme`,
`license` and `requires-python` are recommended. `authors` or `maintainers`,
`urls` and `classifiers` are looked for as well. A missing field from these
two groups is a note, and so is a value that cannot be right, such as a
version that is not a valid version or a `readme` file that does not exist. A
field listed in `dynamic` counts as present. A `[tool.poetry]` table is read
when there is no `[project]` table. Metadata kept only in `setup.py` or
`setup.cfg` is a warning.

This check is never skipped. It is the one that reports a `pyproject.toml`
that is missing or cannot be read, a missing `[project]` table, a missing
`version`, and a `[project]` table whose `requires-python` is missing or
invalid. The other checks that need one of these do not repeat the problem.
They are skipped with the [skip reason](rules.qmd#skip-reasons)
`prerequisite-failed`.

One field is left to another check. For a legacy `[tool.poetry]` table this
check does not list a missing `requires-python`. The
[`python_versions`](#python_versions) check reports it.

### py_typed

Looks for the `py.typed` marker file. Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) 561
asks for it in a package that ships type annotations. No options.

The check samples at most 20 files of a package that has no marker. It gives
a note only when at least half of the public functions in the sample are
annotated. A package below that mark needs no marker, so it is skipped with
the message `py.typed not needed (package is not clearly typed)`. A project
with no package directory, such as a single module, is skipped as well. The
skip reason is `not-applicable` in both cases.

When a file of the sample cannot be parsed and no public function was counted
in the rest, the check is skipped with the message
`Could not parse the package source` and the skip reason `parse-failed`.
Correct the syntax error that the detail line names, or run pycmdcheck with
the Python version the package is written for. Once a function was counted,
the result comes from the files that were read, and the detail line names the
ones left out.

### python_versions

Checks that `requires-python` does not allow a Python version that has
reached its end of life. No options.

The check uses the published end-of-life dates and waits 180 days after a
version's date before it reports that version. Most packages still allow a
version in the months after it retires, and the wait keeps the check from
reporting them on the first day. Python 3.10 reached its end of life on
2026-10-01, so it is reported from 2027-03-30. Until then
`requires-python = ">=3.10"` passes.

A requirement that allows a reported version is a note. The value is also
read from `[tool.poetry]`, `setup.cfg` and `setup.py`.

The check is skipped when it finds no value to judge in any of these places.

| Situation | Skip reason |
|-----------|-------------|
| The `[project]` table has no `requires-python`, or one that is not a valid version specifier | `prerequisite-failed` |
| `pyproject.toml` cannot be read | `prerequisite-failed` |
| `pyproject.toml` is missing or has no `[project]` table, and neither `setup.py` nor `setup.cfg` holds the metadata | `prerequisite-failed` |
| `requires-python` is listed in `dynamic`, or `setup.py` computes the value when it runs | `not-applicable` |

The `metadata` check reports the first three. A constraint kept in a legacy
`[tool.poetry]` table, in `setup.cfg` or in `setup.py` is judged by this
check, so there a missing or invalid value gets a note from it.

For a legacy `[tool.poetry]` table the `metadata` check leaves
`requires-python` out of its list of missing recommended fields, so a missing
`python` entry is reported once, by this check.

### structure

Checks that the project holds an importable package or module. No options.

It accepts a src layout (`src/package/`), a flat layout (`package/`), a
`lib/` or `python/` source directory, a source directory named by the build
backend, a single-file module, a namespace package (PEP 420) and a stub-only
package. Directories of Rust, C or front-end sources under `src/` are ignored.
A directory in the project root whose name starts with an underscore, such as
`_build` or `_vendor`, is not taken for a namespace package unless the build
settings name it. A package that lies only under `_build` is therefore an
error. A package list can name such a directory. So can a setuptools
`packages.find` include pattern that itself starts with an underscore, such
as `_acme*`. The pattern counts only when setuptools would collect the
directory. No exclude pattern may match it, `where`, when set, must include
the project root, and the search must take in namespace packages.
`namespaces = false` in `pyproject.toml` and `packages = find:` in
`setup.cfg` turn that off.

When no package or module is found, the result is an error, with three
exceptions.

- A project that builds a native extension is skipped with the skip reason
  `not-applicable`, because the build makes the module. The check goes by a
  native build backend or build tool in `[build-system]`, extension modules
  declared for setuptools, or a `Cargo.toml`, `CMakeLists.txt` or
  `meson.build` file.
- A project whose `src/` holds only sources in another language, with no
  such sign of a native build, gets a note.
- A project that has only a script in its root, such as `noxfile.py`, or a
  package in a directory that none of the layouts above covers, gets a note.
  Python files in a directory with no `__init__.py` do not count, and that
  project is an error.

A package directory with no `__init__.py` anywhere in it is a warning.

### test_suite

Looks for the project's tests without running them. No options.

The check looks in these places, in this order, and stops at the first one
that holds tests.

1. A `tests` or `test` directory in the project root.
2. A `tests` or `test` directory inside the package.
3. A directory named by `testpaths` in the pytest configuration. That setting
   is read from `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, `tox.ini` or `setup.cfg`. In
   `pyproject.toml` it may be in the table `[tool.pytest.ini_options]` or in
   `[tool.pytest]`, which pytest 9 reads. An entry is taken as the name of a
   directory, so an entry with a wildcard is not used. At most 20 entries
   are looked at.
4. A file named `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, `test.py` or `tests.py` in the
   project root.
5. A file named `test_*.py`, `*_test.py` or `tests.py` anywhere else in the
   project. Hidden directories are not searched, and a file under
   `site-packages` or `node_modules` does not count, because it belongs to
   another project.

A directory counts only when it holds a test module, at any depth. A test
module is a Python file whose name does not start with an underscore and is
not `conftest.py`. An empty `tests/` directory is not a test suite, and
neither is one that holds only `__init__.py`, shared fixtures or data files.
Directory names are matched in any letter case. A symbolic link to a
directory is not followed, so the check never looks outside the project.

A project with tests gets the message `Test suite present`, and a detail line
names the place, for example `Found tests: tests/`. A project with none gets
a warning with the code `test_suite.missing` and the message `No tests found`.

The check reports that tests are present and nothing more. It does not run
them and does not read what they cover. The [`tests`](#tests) check runs
them. Both checks use the same search, so they always agree on whether there
is a suite. Because it only reads files, `test_suite` is part of the `triage`
profile, and `tests` is not.

### tests

Runs the project's test suite.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `runner` | `"pytest"`, `"unittest"` | `"pytest"` | Test runner |
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for the runner |
| `timeout` | positive number | `300` | Seconds the test run may take |

```toml
tests = { runner = "pytest", args = ["-x", "--tb=short"] }
```

The check returns one of these results for a run with pytest.

| What happened | Status | Message |
|---------------|--------|---------|
| Every test passed | ok | `All tests passed` |
| A test failed | error | `Tests failed` |
| pytest could not collect the tests and exited with code 2, for example because a test module cannot be imported | error | `Tests could not be collected` |
| pytest collected no tests | warning | `No tests collected` |
| pytest had an internal error or a usage error, which are exit codes 3 and 4 | warning | `pytest could not run` |

A suite that cannot be collected is an error because pytest stopped before it
ran the tests, which is not a pass. The detail lines show the end of pytest's
own report. The last row is the shared rule for a tool that
[could not run](#tool-could-not-run).

The check is skipped in two cases and starts no test runner in either.

| Situation | Message | Skip reason |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| The project has no tests | `No tests to run` | `prerequisite-failed` |
| pytest is not installed | `pytest not installed` | `tool-missing` |

A project with no tests is a real shortcoming, and it still gets a warning.
The [`test_suite`](#test_suite) check gives it, with the code
`test_suite.missing`, so the cause is reported once. This check has nothing
to run and points at `test_suite` in a detail line. The search for tests
comes first, so a project with no tests is skipped whatever `runner` says.

With `runner = "unittest"` the check runs `python -m unittest discover` with
the `python` found on `PATH`, or `python3` when there is no `python`. Failing
tests are an error there as well. A run that ends before any test, or with a
usage error, is a warning with the message `unittest could not run`.

### typing

Runs a type checker over the package.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `tool` | `"auto"`, `"mypy"`, `"pyright"` | `"auto"` | Type checker to run |
| `strict` | boolean | `false` | Pass `--strict` to mypy |
| `args` | list of strings | `[]` | Extra arguments for the type checker |
| `timeout` | positive number | `300` | Seconds the type checker may run |

```toml
typing = { tool = "mypy", strict = true }
```

With `tool = "auto"` the check looks for a type checker the project has
configured, in this order.

1. mypy, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.mypy]` table, when the project
   has a `mypy.ini` or `.mypy.ini` file, or when `setup.cfg` has a `[mypy]`
   section.
2. pyright, when `pyproject.toml` has a `[tool.pyright]` table, or when the
   project has a `pyrightconfig.json` file.

A project with neither is skipped with the message
`No type checker configured` and the skip reason `not-configured`. Under
`--profile strict` the tool is mypy with `--strict`, whatever the project has
configured and whatever `tool` says here.

Type errors are an error, and the details list the first 10. When pyright
ends with exit code 1, its warnings are listed with the errors and counted
apart in the message, as in `Found 1 type error(s) and 2 warning(s)`. When
the check can read no line of the output, for example because `args` asks
the tool for JSON, the message is `Found some type error(s)` and the details
show the end of the tool's standard output, at most 10 lines.

A type checker that [could not run](#tool-could-not-run) is a warning, with
the message `mypy could not run` or `pyright could not run`. That covers a
problem in the tool's configuration and a package layout that mypy cannot
analyze.

`strict` applies to mypy only, also when `"auto"` chose mypy. pyright has no
`--strict` flag, so with pyright the option is not passed on and a detail
line says so. Turn on pyright's strict mode with
`typeCheckingMode = "strict"` in `[tool.pyright]` or in `pyrightconfig.json`.

### urls

Requests each `http` or `https` address in `[project.urls]` and reports the
ones that do not answer. This check uses the network.

| Option | Values | Default | Description |
|--------|--------|---------|-------------|
| `timeout` | number from 1 to 30 | `10` | Seconds to wait for each request |

```toml
urls = { timeout = 5 }
```

A `timeout` below 1 is raised to 1 and one above 30 is lowered to 30. The
check requests at most 20 addresses and stops after 60 seconds in total. An
address that answers 404 or 410, or whose host name does not exist, is a
warning. One that could not be verified, for example because of a timeout or a
403 answer, is a note. When two or more hosts were tried and none answered,
the check is skipped with the message
`Network unavailable, project URLs not checked` and the skip reason
`network-unavailable`.

The check is also skipped when it has no address to request.

| Situation | Skip reason |
|-----------|-------------|
| The project declares no URLs, lists `urls` in `dynamic`, or has no `http` or `https` address on a public host | `not-applicable` |
| `pyproject.toml` is missing, cannot be read, has no `[project]` table, or has a `urls` value that is not a table | `prerequisite-failed` |

The `metadata` check reports the cases of the second row. A `[project.urls]`
table that holds a value other than a string is a note, and no address is
requested.

#### Local and Private Hosts

The check does not contact a host on your own machine or your own network. No
request is made when the host of an address is `localhost`, is empty, or
resolves to an address that is not globally routable. That covers loopback
addresses such as `127.0.0.1`, private ranges such as `10.0.0.0/8` and
`192.168.0.0/16`, link-local addresses such as `169.254.169.254`, the shared
range `100.64.0.0/10`, and reserved, multicast and unspecified addresses.

The host is tested as it is written and as it reads once its percent escapes
are decoded, so `http://%31%32%37.0.0.1/` is refused like `http://127.0.0.1/`.
The same test is applied to every redirect, so a public address that
redirects to a private one is not followed.

The check connects to the address it tested. For each request it looks the
host name up once, refuses the request if one of the addresses is local or
private, and opens the connection to one of those same addresses. The name is
not looked up a second time, so a name server cannot give one answer to the
test and another to the connection.

A redirect is followed only to another `http` or `https` address. A redirect
that leads anywhere else, to an `ftp` address for example, is not followed,
and the host it names is not looked up. The address is listed as
`could not verify: redirects to a URL that is not http or https` and counts
as one that could not be verified.

An address that was left out is listed as
`not checked (local or private address)`. It counts as neither unreachable nor
unverified, and the numbers in the message leave it out. This is
`pycmdcheck --check urls --verbose` on a package whose two project URLs are
local. No address was requested, so the check is skipped with the reason
`not-applicable`.

```
│  ○  │ urls  │ No public project URLs to check │ 0.01s │
└─────┴───────┴─────────────────────────────────┴───────┘

urls details:
  Documentation: http://localhost:8000/ not checked (local or private address)
  Dashboard: http://127.0.0.1:8000/status not checked (local or private address)
```

The only switch is the environment variable `PYCMDCHECK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_URLS`.
Set it to `1` in the environment that runs pycmdcheck, and local and private
addresses are requested like any other. The rule for redirects stays in
force. There is no option for this in `pyproject.toml` and none on the command
line, because the files of the checked project are not trusted. A project
cannot set the variable.

One case is left. When a request goes through a proxy, the proxy looks the
name up and opens the connection. The check still tests the name with a
lookup of its own, and it cannot hold the proxy to the address it tested.
Python takes a proxy from environment variables such as `https_proxy`, and
from the system settings on macOS and Windows. Do not rely on this rule alone
when you check a repository you do not trust from behind a proxy. The `triage`
profile does not run the `urls` check at all.

### version

Compares the `__version__` written in the package with the `version` in
`pyproject.toml`. No options.

Two versions that differ are an error. The comparison follows PEP 440, the
Python standard for version numbers, so `1.0` equals `1.0.0`. The result is
ok only when two versions written out in the files were compared and agree.

A project with nothing to compare is skipped.

| Situation | Skip reason |
|-----------|-------------|
| `version` is listed in `dynamic` | `not-applicable` |
| No package or module was found, or the code has no `__version__` | `not-applicable` |
| `__version__` is set when the code runs, for example by a call to `importlib.metadata.version()` or by an import from another module | `not-applicable` |
| `__version__` is written as a number or a tuple, such as `1.0` or `(1, 0)`. The message is `__version__ is not a string`. | `not-applicable` |
| `pyproject.toml` is missing, cannot be read, has no `[project]` table, or has no `version` | `prerequisite-failed` |

The `metadata` check reports the cases of the last row.

When the file that should hold `__version__` cannot be parsed, the check is
skipped with the message `Could not read __version__ from code` and the skip
reason `parse-failed`. Correct the syntax error that the detail line names,
or run pycmdcheck with the Python version the package is written for.

## Statuses Each Check Can Return

| Check | Statuses |
|-------|----------|
| `build` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `changelog` | ok, note, warning |
| `ci` | ok, note |
| `citation` | ok, note |
| `community` | ok, note |
| `dependencies` | ok, note, warning, skipped |
| `docs` | ok, note, warning, skipped |
| `doctests` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `formatting` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `license` | ok, note, warning |
| `linting` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `metadata` | ok, note, warning, error |
| `py_typed` | ok, note, skipped |
| `python_versions` | ok, note, skipped |
| `structure` | ok, note, warning, error, skipped |
| `test_suite` | ok, warning |
| `tests` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `typing` | ok, warning, error, skipped |
| `urls` | ok, note, warning, skipped |
| `version` | ok, error, skipped |

One rule decides between two of these statuses. A check that did not look at
anything is skipped, and its [skip reason](rules.qmd#skip-reasons) says why.
A note always names something the author of the package can improve.

Every note, warning and error carries at least one rule code, and
[Rule Codes](rules.qmd#rules-of-each-check) lists the codes of each check with
the status they carry. The deprecated [`imports`](#imports) check is always
skipped and has no row here.

Two more cases apply to every check. A check that raises an exception is
reported as an error, and a check that `--fail-fast` did not start is reported
as skipped with the skip reason `fail-fast`.

## Complete Example

```toml
[tool.pycmdcheck]
fail_on = ["warning"]

[tool.pycmdcheck.checks]
tests = { runner = "pytest", args = ["-x"], timeout = 600 }
# A named tool runs whether or not the project has configured it.
linting = { tool = "ruff", args = ["--select", "E,F,W,I"] }
typing = { tool = "mypy", strict = true }
formatting = { tool = "ruff" }
docs = { check_readme_sections = true, min_docstring_coverage = 80 }
build = { timeout = 300 }
urls = { timeout = 5 }
doctests = false
citation = false
```

## A Settings File Outside the Project {#config-file}

`pycmdcheck --config FILE` takes the profile, the checks and their options
from `FILE` and does not read the `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of the directory
it checks. The file is for someone who checks repositories they do not own,
such as a review bot or an organization with one standard for all its
packages. They cannot put settings into those repositories, so the file is
kept in a repository of their own, where a change to it can be reviewed.
pycmdcheck does not test where the file is. A file inside the checked
directory is accepted, and it would hand the settings back to that
directory.

The [command-line reference](cli.qmd#config-file) shows a run. It also says
when a profile on the command line is enough, and how `--config` works with
`--check`, with `--skip` and with `--fail-on`. The short form of `--skip` is
`-s`. This section is the reference for the file.

```toml
# Start from the built-in triage profile, which only reads files.
profile = "triage"
fail_on = "warning"

[checks]
citation = false
docs = { check_docs_site = false }
```

That file runs 11 of the 12 checks of the `triage` profile. It leaves
`citation` out, does not ask for documentation beyond the README, and makes
the run fail on warnings as well as on errors.

The file is written in TOML (Tom's Obvious Minimal Language), the format of
`pyproject.toml`. It has to be encoded as UTF-8 (the 8-bit Unicode
Transformation Format) without a byte order mark, and it can be no larger
than 1 mebibyte (MiB), which is 1,048,576 bytes.

### The Keys of the File {#config-file-keys}

| Key | Value | Meaning |
|-----|-------|---------|
| `profile` | `"minimal"`, `"triage"`, `"core"`, `"pyopensci"` or `"strict"` | The built-in [profile](cli.qmd#profiles) the run starts from. Required. |
| `fail_on` | `"error"`, `"warning"` or `"note"`, or a list of them | The status from which the run exits with code 1. Optional. Without it the value is `"error"`. |
| `checks` | A table, written under a `[checks]` line | The checks to take out of the profile and the options to set. Optional. |

Any other key at the top of the file is an error. `profile` and `fail_on`
have to stand above the `[checks]` line, because TOML reads every line below
it as part of that table.

`profile` names one of the built-in profiles. You cannot define a named
profile of your own, in this file or anywhere else, because a name that is
not built in would have to be looked up in the repository being checked. The
deprecated name `default` is not accepted here. Write `core`.

`fail_on` is a threshold, as [`fail_on`](#fail_on) in `pyproject.toml` is. It
may be one word or a list. In a list the least severe status counts, and an
empty list means `"error"`. A `--fail-on` option on the command line wins
over it.

### The checks Table {#config-file-checks}

Each key under `[checks]` is the name of a check that is in the profile. Its
value has one of three forms.

| Entry | What it does |
|--------------|--------------|
| `citation = false` | Takes the check out of the run |
| `citation = true` | Keeps the check. This changes nothing, because the profile runs it already. |
| `docs = { check_docs_site = false }` | Keeps the check and sets options for it |

A table of options may also hold `enabled`. With `enabled = false` the check
is taken out, as it is with `false`.

A file can take checks out of a profile and cannot add one. An entry for a
check that is not in the profile is an error, whatever its value. A custom
check is in no profile, so a file cannot name one. A file that takes out
every check is an error as well.

### Options a File May Set {#config-file-options}

| Check | Options |
|-------|--------------------------|
| `build` | `args`, `timeout` |
| `docs` | `require_readme`, `check_readme_sections`, `check_docs_site`, `check_docstrings`, `min_docstring_coverage` |
| `doctests` | `args`, `timeout` |
| `formatting` | `tool`, `args`, `timeout` |
| `linting` | `tool`, `args`, `timeout` |
| `tests` | `runner`, `args`, `timeout` |
| `typing` | `tool`, `strict`, `args`, `timeout` |
| `urls` | `timeout` |

The other 12 checks have no option besides `enabled`. The sections under
[Per-Check Options](#per-check-options) say what each option does and give
its default.

A settings file is read strictly. The `[tool.pycmdcheck]` table of a project
is read with tolerance, as [Basic Configuration](#basic-configuration)
describes. There a wrong value is ignored, moved into its range, or reported
in the result of the check. In a settings file each of these is an error,
and no check runs.

- An option that the check does not have.
- A value of the wrong type.
- A value outside its range.

| Option | Value a settings file accepts |
|--------------------|--------------------|
| `require_readme`, `check_readme_sections`, `check_docs_site`, `check_docstrings`, `strict`, `enabled` | `true` or `false`. A string such as `"no"` is refused. |
| `min_docstring_coverage` | A number from 0 to 100 |
| `tool`, `runner` | One of the values that the section of the check lists |
| `args` | A list of strings. It may be empty. |
| `timeout` of the six [tool checks](#options-shared-by-the-tool-checks) | A number above 0 and at most 86400 |
| `timeout` of `urls` | A number from 1 to 30 |

`true` and `false` do not count as numbers.

### The Order of the Options {#config-file-order}

The options of a run with `--config` are put together in three steps, and a
later step wins.

1. The built-in defaults. They are pytest as the test runner and `"auto"` for
   the linter, the type checker and the formatter.
2. The options of the profile.
3. The options of the file.

A file can therefore change an option that its profile sets. With
`profile = "triage"`, the entry `docs = { min_docstring_coverage = 80 }`
turns the docstring scan on, although the profile turns it off.

Nothing in this order comes from the checked project. Its `[tool.pycmdcheck]`
table is not read. It supplies no option, no enable flag and no `fail_on`,
and no warning about a malformed entry in it is printed.

The checks still read the other files of the project, which is their job.
With `tool = "auto"`, for example, the `linting`, `typing` and `formatting`
checks find the tool from the project's own configuration files, as
[Choosing the Tool](#tool-auto) describes.

### Mistakes in the File {#config-file-errors}

A mistake in the file is a usage error. pycmdcheck exits with code 2 before
any check runs and prints nothing on standard output. After its two usage
lines it writes one line to standard error. The line starts with
`Error: Config file`, names the file as it was given, and says what is
wrong. `--exit-zero` does not change the exit code. The first mistake that is
found ends the run, so a file with two mistakes takes two runs to correct.

| Mistake | Message |
|----------|---------------|
| The file is larger than 1 MiB, or `FILE` is not a regular file, for example a device | `The file could not be read (larger than 1 MiB).` or `The file could not be read (not a regular file).` |
| The file is not UTF-8 | `The file is not valid UTF-8.` |
| The file starts with a byte order mark | `The file starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark, which TOML does not allow.` |
| The file is not valid TOML | `The file is not valid TOML. Invalid value (at line 1, column 11).` The second sentence is the parser's. |
| A key at the top of the file is not one of the three. A `pyproject.toml` passed by mistake ends here. | `Unknown key(s) build-system, project. A config file holds profile, fail_on and a [checks] table.` |
| There is no `profile` | `The file names no profile. Add a line such as profile = "triage" above [checks]. The profiles are minimal, triage, core, pyopensci, strict.` |
| The `profile` line is below `[checks]` | `The profile line is below [checks], where it is read as a check. Move it above [checks].` |
| `profile` is not a built-in profile | `profile must be one of minimal, triage, core, pyopensci, strict, but it is "house".` |
| `fail_on` is not a status | `fail_on must be error, warning or note, or a list of them, but it is "fatal".` |
| `checks` is not a table | `checks must be a table, but it is "all".` |
| A name under `[checks]` is not an installed check | `Unknown check licence in [checks].` The message then lists the checks of the profile. For a `fail_on` line below `[checks]` it also says to move the line. |
| A check is not in the profile | `tests is not in the profile triage. A config file can take a check out of a profile and cannot add one.` |
| An entry is not `true`, `false` or a table | `docs must be true, false or a table of options, but it is 3.` |
| A check does not have the option | `Unknown option colour for the check docs. Its options are enabled, require_readme, check_readme_sections, check_docs_site, check_docstrings, min_docstring_coverage.` |
| A value has the wrong type | `docs.check_docstrings must be true or false, but it is "no".` |
| A value is outside its range | `urls.timeout must be a number from 1 to 30, but it is 31.` |
| An item of `args` is not a string | `tests.args must be a list of strings, but it holds 2.` |
| The file leaves no check | `The file leaves no check to run.` |

A message shows a value as it is written in TOML, so a string appears in
double quotes. `pycmdcheck --config FILE --list` reads the file and runs no
check, which makes it a quick test of a file that has changed.

A `FILE` that does not exist, is a directory or cannot be opened for reading
is refused before pycmdcheck looks into it. The exit code is 2 as well, and
the last line on standard error has another form. Its end is
`does not exist.`, `is a directory.` or `is not readable.`, and this is the
first of the three.

```
Error: Invalid value for '--config': File '.github/pycmdcheck-triage.toml' does not exist.
```
